# Effectiveness of father-inclusive interventions on maternal, paternal, couples, and early child outcomes in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review

**Authors:** Joshua Jeong; Eileen F. Sullivan; Juliet K. McCann

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Global Health and Population, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | bHarvard Graduate School of Education, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Most caregiving interventions for young children are directed to female caregivers. Relatively few have included male caregivers as program participants especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The range of potential benefits that can be achieved through the engagement of fathers and male caregivers has not been adequately explored from a family systems perspective. We reviewed interventions that engaged male caregivers to support young children in LMICs and summarized impacts on maternal, paternal, couples, and child outcomes. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Global Health Library for quantitative evaluation studies of social and behavioral interventions that included fathers or other male caregivers to improve nurturing care for young children under 5 years of age in LMICs. Three authors independently extracted data using a structured form. Forty-four articles, representing 33 intervention evaluations, were included. The most common type of intervention targeted fathers along with their female partners and primarily to address child nutrition and health. Across interventions, maternal outcomes were the most evaluated outcomes (82%), followed by paternal (58%), couple’s relationship (48%) and child-level outcomes (45%). Overall, father-inclusive interventions had positive impacts on maternal, paternal and couples’ relationship outcomes. Although there was greater variation in the degree of supportive evidence for child outcomes compared to maternal, paternal, and couples outcomes, findings suggested mostly positive effects across all outcomes. Limitations included relatively weak study designs and heterogeneity across interventions, outcome types, and measurement tools. Interventions that include fathers and other male caregivers have potential to improve maternal and paternal caregiving, couple’s relationships dynamics, and early child outcomes in LMICs. More evaluation studies, using rigorous methods and robust measurement frameworks, are needed to bolster this evidence-base about the effect of fathers’ engagement for young children, caregivers, and families in LMICs.

## Introduction

Over the past two decades, there has been increasing recognition globally and across various sectors about the importance of engaging fathers and other male caregivers in nurturing care interventions for young children (Plan International & Promundo, 2021; World Health Organization, 2015). Nurturing care interventions refer to those that broadly aim to promote caregivers’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices pertaining to child health, nutrition, early learning, responsive caregiving, and safety and security (Black et al., 2017). With recent sociodemographic transitions and economic development – coupled with increased labor migration and urbanization that also have contributed to the nuclearization of families (Odimegwu et al., 2020) – more male caregivers co-reside with their children today than ever before, with an estimated 70% of children in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) living in the same household as their mother and father (F. S. Martin & Zulaika, 2016). These changes in family structures, coupled with positive shifts in social norms and gender equity, have contributed to increased father involvement with young children (Kato-Wallace et al., 2014).

Informed by frameworks spanning from developmental psychology to gender studies, there are various ways through which fathers and other male caregivers have been shown to positively influence outcomes (Cabrera et al., 2018). For example, family systems theory highlights how fatherhood is embedded within socioecological contexts that encompass not only men individually but also inextricably their relationship dynamics with their children and partners (Cox & Paley, 1997). Indeed, research has documented how father involvement can benefit fathers in terms of their own caregiving knowledge and childcare practices(Lee et al., 2018; Panter-Brick et al., 2014), their partners’ (i.e., maternal) caregiving capacities (Tokhi et al., 2018; Yourkavitch et al., 2017), couple’s relationship dynamics such as the coparenting relationship or supportive behaviors (Lee et al., 2018; Tokhi et al., 2018), and ultimately child outcomes (Panter-Brick et al., 2014; Tokhi et al., 2018). Furthermore, considering the prevailing patriarchal norms in many LMICs, gender-transformative efforts to collaboratively engage men can facilitate greater women’s empowerment and more equitable couple’s relationships and gender attitudes, which in turn can also shape child outcomes (Comrie-Thomson et al., 2015; Kato-Wallace et al., 2014). Despite this growing evidence about the importance and potential of father involvement globally, the vast majority of the early childhood intervention literature pertains to mothers (Britto et al., 2017) and/or studies mostly conducted in high-income countries (Henrich et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2018).

Several prior systematic reviews have aimed to address these evidence gaps and have documented the effectiveness of engaging fathers in caregiving interventions to support young children in LMICs. However, these previous reviews have investigated male caregiver engagement in the context of particular types of interventions, such as specifically maternal and child nutrition interventions (S. L. Martin et al., 2020; Tadesse et al., 2018) or maternal and child health interventions (Tokhi et al., 2018). Furthermore, most prior reviews of father involvement interventions in LMICs have summarized program effectiveness primarily with regards to maternal (e.g., caregiving knowledge, childcare and feeding practices) and/or child outcomes (e.g., infant nutrition, mortality) (Brusamento et al., 2012; Yourkavitch et al., 2017). Relatively few reviews have investigated program effects beyond the mother and child to additionally include couples’ relationship dynamics (Mahesh et al., 2018; Tokhi et al., 2018) as well as paternal outcomes (e.g., fathers’ caregiving knowledge, attitudes, and practices). Therefore, in this systematic review, we use broad inclusion criteria to include interventions that have involved male caregivers in any type of nurturing care for young children in the first five years of life in LMICs. We apply a family systems perspective (Cox & Paley, 1997) to examine the effects of father-inclusive interventions on outcomes pertaining to multiple individuals, specifically mothers, fathers, couples, and young children.

## Methods

### Search strategy

This systematic review was conducted and reported using the PRISMA guidelines. This review was preregistered in PROSPERO (CRD42022310288). We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Global Health Library for peer-reviewed articles published from database inception until March 7, 2022. We used a string of search terms that combined keywords relating to program evaluation, male caregivers, nurturing care, early childhood, and LMICs. See Supplementary Methods Text for search string used in PubMed as an example.

### Study selection

Full-text articles were included if they met the following criteria: represented social and behavioral interventions that aimed to improve caregivers’ knowledge, attitudes, practices, or skills pertaining to nurturing care for young children (i.e., health, nutrition, responsive caregiving, safety and security, early learning) (Black et al., 2017); included any male caregivers as participants of the program (e.g., fathers, uncles, male partner of child’s mother, or another man involved in the life of the child or mother); used a quantitative evaluation design; focused on caregivers of children who were younger than aged 5 years; and conducted in a LMIC. Studies were excluded if the intervention did not include any message pertaining to caregiving of young children (e.g., interventions focused on family planning or HIV prevention only without any additional nurturing care message) or did not actively include any male caregivers as program participants.

### Data extraction

Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of each study identified in the systematic search using the web-based platform Covidence. Full text articles were reviewed to determine eligibility. Any disagreements between the reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus. Reference lists of included studies were scanned for any additional relevant studies that may have been missed from the electronic search. Three reviewers independently extracted data from each eligible study using a structured extraction form in Excel. The team was trained on how to use the extraction form, which was refined through a process whereby each analyst piloted the form against 6 relevant articles. The first author cross-checked the extractions between reviewers and facilitated weekly team meetings throughout the data extraction process to address any questions, resolve any discrepancies in data extractions between reviewers through group discussion and consensus, and monitor study progress. For the present review, data were extracted on the outcome measures used across studies and program impact results. In a separate review, we extracted and reported results about the implementation approaches used across these father-inclusive interventions (e.g., delivery strategies, intervention content, implementation barriers and enablers) (Jeong et al., 2023).

### Outcomes

We applied a family systems perspective to our conceptualization of how the influence of fathers on young children can involve multiple relationships and individuals. Thus, we examined four broad categories of outcomes: maternal, paternal, couples, and child-level outcomes. Then, we used a qualitative inductive approach to create sub-categories of outcomes that were thematically similar (e.g., maternal parenting, psychosocial wellbeing). These thematic categories were iteratively refined over the course of analysis through regular discussions among the three reviewers. We described outcomes as reported by the study authors. Regarding the timing of the outcome measurement, we extracted only one timepoint for a given effect and that which aligned most closely to the completion of the program (i.e., endline).

### Quality assessment

Two reviewers independently assessed the methodological quality of each included study according to the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklists for randomized control trials (RCT) and quasi-experimental studies (Porritt et al., 2014). The checklists covered various aspects, including whether there was a control group, and if so the degree of similarity between groups, whether outcomes were measured at repeated times, and reliability of measurement approach. Any discrepancies in assessments were resolved through discussion.

### Data synthesis

We conducted a narrative synthesis of the short-term immediate effectiveness of this evidence base in terms of maternal, paternal, couples’, and child-level outcomes, and then within each of these groups furthermore by thematic type of outcome. Each study outcome was coded to one of the following 4 categories: majority positive, if they reported statistically significant (defined at p<0.05) improvements or higher scores for the intervention group relative to the comparison group for more than half of the outcomes in a given thematic domain; marginally positive, if they reported significant improvements for at least one outcome but fewer than the majority (which included cases of a 50–50 even split) of evaluated outcomes in a given domain; null, if all outcomes were null effects; or unclear, if statistical testing was not conducted or data were inadequately reported. Our classification for whether study results were considered “improvements” or beneficial in directionality of effect were based on numeric values and how the authors themselves hypothesized, described, or interpreted their study results.

## Results

A total of 6,977 articles were identified through the electronic database search with 8 additional articles identified elsewhere. In total, 44 articles – representing 33 different intervention evaluations – met inclusion criteria for this systematic review (Figure 1). The publication years spanned from 1999 to 2021. There has been a marked increase in studies over time (annualize growth rate of 8.0%) with approximately half published recently since 2018.

Table 1 summarizes characteristics of included studies. Approximately half were conducted in Sub-Saharan Africa (46%). About half used an RCT evaluation design (51%) compared to roughly one-third that used a quasi-experimental design (36%) or one-eighth that used a non-experimental study design (12%). While all studies had male caregivers as program participants to some degree, the “unit” for recruitment and which caregiver(s) was enrolled specifically by design did vary across studies: 42.4% enrolled couples, 21.2% the mother only, 21.2% any primary caregiver, and 15.2% the father only. As for the types of participating male caregivers across these interventions, three in four interventions (76%) referred to the male caregivers as fathers specifically, compared to 6.1% of interventions in which male caregivers were the married husbands of pregnant women (not explicitly defined as the child’s father), 6.1% of programs referred to any male caregiver of the child (e.g., father/grandfather/uncle), and 12.1% that most broadly referred to any male caregiver with respect to the mother and/or child (e.g., current male partner/father/uncle). Since most of the male caregivers across the studies were described as fathers specifically, we use the term “fathers” hereon when referring to male caregivers broadly.

In the majority of studies, fathers participated in the interventions jointly together with their partners (i.e., couples), compared to other studies in which fathers participated on their own and entirely separately from mothers (24%) or with more mixture and alongside other primary caregivers of the child (i.e., mostly mothers but also some fathers, 18%). All studies involving couples were in heterosexual relationships. In three of the studies with couples, some households (less than half across all cases) were in polygamous marriages (Carneiro et al., 2021; Daniele et al., 2018; Heath et al., 2020).

All interventions were multicomponent and most frequently promoted messages pertaining to child nutrition (79%) and health (70%). Some also addressed other content with fathers including parenting (36%), psychosocial wellbeing (27%), and violence prevention (21%). See elsewhere for more details about program model characteristics, curriculum content, behavior change techniques used, and implementation barriers and enablers faced across these interventions with fathers (Jeong et al., 2023).

In terms of outcomes evaluated, 82% of interventions (n=27) measured at least one maternal outcome; 58% (n=19) measured at least one paternal outcome; 48% (n=16) measured at least one outcome about couple’s relationship dynamics; and 45% (n=15) measured at least one child-level outcome. Regarding the type of caregiver(s) who was surveyed for the evaluation, 42% of studies systematically interviewed couples, or both the mother and father, who in all such cases were each interviewed separately; compared to the majority that collected data from only one caregiver per household: any primary caregiver of the child who represented mostly mothers (21%), mothers specifically (18%), or fathers specifically (15%) (Table 1).

Using JBI’s critical appraisal checklist tools, the methodological weaknesses most frequently identified in the included RCTs related to lack of blinding of participants (0% compliance) and delivery agents (0%) and lack of reliability in outcome measurement (24%) (Supplementary Table 1). In the quasi-experimental studies, the main methodological concerns related to inadequate reporting and analysis of participant follow up (19%) and lack of reliability in outcome measurement (25%) (Supplementary Table 2).

Figure 2 represents a heatmap of the degree of supportive evidence regarding intervention effectiveness for the various outcomes across all studies included in this review. Any shaded cell highlights that at least one outcome for that type was assessed in a given study (with different colors associated with varying strengths of evidence; see legend), whereas unshaded or blank cells correspond to the absence of any such outcome measurement. Of the 119 total reported outcome types across the studies, approximately half reflected positive effects (55%), with the remaining being marginally positive (18%), null (17%), or unclear due lack of statistical analysis or inadequate reporting (10%). None of the interventions reported any harmful effects.

### Maternal outcomes

Twenty-seven interventions (82%) measured program impacts on maternal outcomes (Supplementary Table 3). Maternal outcomes were more commonly assessed in interventions that by design recruited mothers or couples at the program outset, compared to those that recruited fathers specifically (40%). The types of maternal outcomes and details about the specific measures referenced are presented in Supplementary Table 4. Various domains were evaluated (i.e, maternal caregiving for nutrition, caregiving for health, parenting, maternal psychosocial wellbeing), and within a given domain, there was heterogeneity in the specific measurement tools used and degree to which they were reported across studies. However, overall results suggested mostly positive effects of father engagement programs across all domains of maternal outcomes. Twenty-two of these intervention evaluations measured outcomes directly from and about mothers specifically, but a separate 5 studies more broadly sampled and asked about outcomes regarding any one primary caregiver of the child (Betancourt et al., 2020; Heath et al., 2020; Lakkis et al., 2020; Skar et al., 2021; Sokolovic et al., 2022). Given that these 5 studies did not disaggregate results by specific caregiver type and the samples were mostly represented by mothers, we refer to the results of this collective set of studies as maternal outcomes.

Of the 15 interventions that assessed mothers’ caregiving for nutrition (e.g., maternal knowledge, attitudes, and practices about breastfeeding), 11 reported positive effects. For example, intervention mothers reported higher rates of exclusive breastfeeding (Bich et al., 2016; Bich et al., 2014; Bich et al., 2019; Carneiro et al., 2021; Daniele et al., 2018; Ozlüses & Celebioglu, 2014; Su & Ouyang, 2016; Susin & Giugliani, 2008; Turan et al., 2018; Verma et al., 2017) and dietary diversity (Nguyen et al., 2017), and lower odds of feeding infants with supplemental foods (Sahip & Molzan Turan, 2007). One intervention by Downs et al. (2019) that sent voice messages to both mothers and fathers about infant feeding reported marginally positive results, with improvements in mothers’ attitudes towards child feeding, but no changes in continued breastfeeding at 6 months. Two interventions found null results on exclusive breastfeeding (Hazra et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2018). Finally, one intervention did not present statistical analyses, but reported slight improvements in exclusive breastfeeding (Turan et al., 2001).

Of the 14 interventions to assess mothers’ caregiving for health (e.g., health seeking behaviors for child, family planning methods), 9 reported a majority of positive effects, including improvements in antenatal care attendance (Carneiro et al., 2021; Doyle et al., 2018; Mullany et al., 2007; Nguyen et al., 2017; Rahman et al., 2019), women’s use of modern contraceptive methods (Daniele et al., 2018), maternal preventative practices for child health (Singla et al., 2015), and child healthcare seeking practices (Betancourt et al., 2020). Two interventions reported marginally positive results, for example, with one study indicating greater maternal healthcare seeking for child diarrhea but no difference in healthcare seeking for child fever or pneumonia (Swigart et al., 2019). Turan et al. (2018) delivered home-based educational visits to couples in Kenya and found improvements in mothers’ attendance of postpartum checkups but no differences in family postpartum planning. Other interventions reported null results on maternal ART adherence (Jones et al., 2018) and current use of a modern contraceptive method (Sahip & Molzan Turan, 2007). One final intervention did not report statistical tests, but showed trends of improvements in use of a modern family planning method (Turan et al., 2001).

Nine interventions evaluated outcomes pertaining to maternal parenting practices. Six interventions reported mostly positive effects on maternal parenting outcomes, such as improved knowledge of child development (Singla et al., 2015), stimulation practices (Abimpaye et al., 2019; Betancourt et al., 2020; Singla et al., 2015), and reduced child physical maltreatment (Abimpaye et al., 2019; Doyle et al., 2018; Lakkis et al., 2020). One intervention showed marginally positive results, with intervention households engaged in less child physical maltreatment, but no difference in psychological aggression (Heath et al., 2020). One intervention found no significant differences in mothers’ parenting knowledge or practices between interventions that invited fathers and those with mothers only (Luoto et al., 2021). The remaining intervention reported no differences in child physical abuse (Skar et al., 2021).

Seven interventions assessed maternal psychosocial wellbeing outcomes. Four interventions reported mostly beneficial effects, such as reduced maternal depression (Betancourt et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2018; Lakkis et al., 2020; Sokolovic et al., 2022) and parenting stress (Lakkis et al., 2020). One intervention found marginally positive effects, such as reduced depressive symptoms and improvements in active ways of coping, but null results on daily stressors and overall ways of coping (Singla et al., 2015). One intervention did not present the between-group differences in caregiver mental health indicators (Skar et al., 2021), while another intervention found no significant differences in maternal depression, stress, social support, or self-efficacy comparing an intervention with couples versus mothers only (Luoto et al., 2021).

### Paternal outcomes

Nineteen interventions (58%) measured program impacts on paternal outcomes (Supplementary Table 5). Paternal outcomes were more commonly assessed in interventions that by design recruited fathers or couples at the program outset, compared to those that recruited mothers specifically (43%). Various domains were evaluated (i.e., paternal parenting, caregiving for nutrition, caregiving for health, psychosocial wellbeing), and within a given domain, there was heterogeneity in the specific measures used and especially for paternal outcome measures pertaining to caregiving for nutrition and health, with no two studies using the same tool/indicator (Supplementary Table 6). Overall, results suggested mostly positive effects of father engagement programs for paternal parenting and paternal caregiving for nutrition, but more mixed results for paternal caregiving for health and paternal psychosocial wellbeing.

For paternal parenting outcomes, 6 found overall beneficial effects, including improvements in fathers’ attachment and stimulation (Abimpaye et al., 2019; Ashburn et al., 2017; L. A. Rempel et al., 2017), other childcare activities (Doyle et al., 2018), and reductions in physical punishment (Ashburn et al., 2017; Doyle et al., 2018). One intervention found positive effects on the indicator of fathers changing the child’s diaper, but no difference for the indicator of fathers playing with the child (Sahip & Molzan Turan, 2007). One intervention found a null effect on paternal stimulation when comparing a couple’s intervention to a mothers only intervention in Kenya (Luoto et al., 2021). The remaining intervention described improvements in fathers’ parenting knowledge, attitudes, and practices in Pakistan, but did not conduct statistical testing (Husain et al., 2021).

Of the 7 interventions to evaluate paternal caregiving for nutrition, 5 reported positive effects for the majority of nutrition outcomes assessed, including improvements in fathers’ knowledge of breastfeeding (Bich & Cuong, 2017; Su & Ouyang, 2016; Susin et al., 1999) and attitudes towards the importance of nutrition during pregnancy and infancy (Downs et al., 2019). The other 2 interventions did not report statistical analyses, but one community-based intervention found improvements in fathers’ breastfeeding knowledge (Turan et al., 2001), while another clinic-based intervention conversely found no difference in fathers’ breastfeeding knowledge (Turan et al., 2001).

Of the 6 interventions that measured impacts on paternal caregiving for health, 2 reported positive effects, such as improved knowledge of newborn care (Hazra et al., 2018) and awareness of maternal health and childbirth (Rahman et al., 2019). One intervention found no differences in fathers’ desired fertility (Sahip & Molzan Turan, 2007). The remaining 3 interventions did not report results from the statistical analyses, but results included improvements in fathers’ health and daily functioning (Husain et al., 2021), knowledge of maternal and infant health (Turan et al., 2001), but no improvements in knowledge of preventative healthcare (Turan et al., 2001).

Of the 4 interventions that measured paternal psychosocial wellbeing, results were inconsistent. One intervention found higher scores in fathers’ self-efficacy with regards to supporting optimal caregiving for nutrition (Nguyen et al., 2018). One intervention found mixed results with intervention fathers reporting less anxiety but no differences in fathers’ stress or self-esteem (Heath et al., 2020). Another intervention found no intervention differences in fathers’ anxiety levels (Sahip & Molzan Turan, 2007). A fathers’ group intervention in Pakistan found reduced paternal depression and stress levels, along with increased paternal social support and self-esteem after the intervention, but statistical testing was not conducted (Husain et al., 2021).

### Couples’ outcomes

Sixteen interventions (48%) evaluated intervention effects on couples’ outcomes (Supplementary Table 7). Couples outcomes were consistently undermeasured irrespective of the type of caregiver(s) that was recruitment into the study (e.g., whether programs enrolled mothers versus couples). Various domains were evaluated (i.e., male partner support for women, couple’s decision-making, intimate partner violence, couple’s communication), and within a given domain, there was heterogeneity in the specific measures used. For example, all studies that measured couple’s relationship quality used different tools (Supplementary Table 8). Overall, results suggested mostly positive effects of father engagement programs for male partner support, but more mixed results for the other domains.

Out of the 10 interventions that measured male partner support for women, 5 interventions reported a majority of positive impacts, including improved paternal support for breastfeeding (Sahip & Molzan Turan, 2007; Sokolovic et al., 2022) and childcare (Doyle et al., 2018). Three interventions reported marginally beneficial results such as on perceived positive partner support but no difference in perceived negative support (Singla et al., 2015), and improved paternal support for complementary feeding but not in support for household chores or buying food for the child (Dinga et al., 2018). Two interventions found null effects such as support for male partner antenatal care attendance (Turan et al., 2018) and mothers’ perceived support from fathers (Luoto et al., 2021).

Of the 5 interventions that assessed couples’ decision making, 2 interventions reported positive impacts, including more equitable decision making about how many children to have (Doyle et al., 2018) and child feeding practices (Dinga et al., 2018). Two other interventions reported a mixture of positive and null results, such as more joint decision making between couples regarding child healthcare seeking, but not child diet (Betancourt et al., 2020). Another intervention found no difference in couples’ financial decision making (Ashburn et al., 2017).

Of the 5 interventions to measure intimate partner violence, 2 studies found significant reductions in women’s physical or sexual violence victimization (Doyle et al., 2018) and men’s attitudes and perpetration of intimate partner violence (Ashburn et al., 2017). Two interventions reported a mixture of beneficial and null results, such as 1 study that found reductions in women’s reports of partner violence victimization but no differences in men’s reports of partner violence perpetration (Betancourt et al., 2020). One intervention noted no intervention effects on intimate partner violence victimization or perpetration, but did not report quantitative results for these outcomes (Skar et al., 2021).

Of the 4 interventions that evaluated couple’s relationship quality, 2 found positive impacts (Daniele et al., 2018; J. K. Rempel et al., 2020), whereas 2 others found null effects on caregivers’ perceptions of relationship quality (Heath et al., 2020; Sokolovic et al., 2022). Finally, benefits on other couple’s relationship outcomes – couples communication skills (Ashburn et al., 2017) and couple’s HIV testing and counseling (Turan et al., 2018) – were also documented in single studies.

### Child outcomes

Fifteen interventions (45%) measured impacts on child outcomes (Supplementary Table 9). Child outcomes were consistently undermeasured irrespective of the type of caregiver(s) that was recruitment into the study. Three main domains were evaluated: child development, nutrition, and health. Child outcome measures were described with relatively more detail (Supplementary Table 10) than parent or couples outcome measures. Overall, results on child outcomes had the most heterogeneity relative to the evidence for maternal, paternal, or couples outcomes.

Eight interventions evaluated child nutritional status, of which 3 found a majority of positive effects on outcomes including dietary diversity (Carneiro et al., 2021; Downs et al., 2019), stunting (Carneiro et al., 2021), and vitamin A supplementation (Sloand et al., 2010). Four interventions reported a mix of positive and null results, such as increased child intake of animal source foods specifically but not rates of achieving minimum dietary diversity (Mukuria et al., 2016) or improved dietary diversity but no difference in height-for-age z-score (Singla et al., 2015). One intervention reported null results on child stunting and dietary diversity (Luoto et al., 2021).

Seven interventions assessed impacts on child developmental outcomes. Four of these interventions found positive effects, such as on children’s language development (Abimpaye et al., 2019; L. A. Rempel et al., 2017; Singla et al., 2015). Two interventions found mixed results (Jensen et al., 2021), such as reductions in children’s total behavioral difficulties and hyperactivity but no differences in emotional problems (Lakkis et al., 2020). The remaining intervention found no significant differences in cognitive, language, or socioemotional development (Luoto et al., 2021).

Of the 6 studies to assess health outcomes in children, 2 found positive effects on multiple indicators (Carneiro et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018), whereas 2 interventions reported a mixture of positive and null results, such as improvements in full immunization but no difference in infant mortality (Sloand et al., 2010). The remaining 3 interventions reported null effects, such as on child illness (Singla et al., 2015), health problems (Sahip & Molzan Turan, 2007), or mortality (Verma et al., 2017).

## Discussion

In this study, we reviewed the effectiveness of interventions that included fathers and other male caregivers to improve caregiving for young children during the first 5 years of life in LMICs. Although several prior reviews have examined the effectiveness of involving fathers in maternal and child health and nutrition interventions (Tadesse et al., 2018; Tokhi et al., 2018), our systematic review adds to this literature by considering a more expansive range of nurturing care interventions (e.g., parenting, violence prevention interventions) and examining various outcomes from a family systems perspective that encompassed program effects on beyond just one individual in a given household. Overall, we identified 33 father-inclusive intervention evaluations that were mostly published in the past five years – highlighting a growing evidence base and priority around engaging fathers in early childhood interventions in LMICs.

Our results revealed benefits for multiple individuals within the family and with respect to various types of outcomes. Half of the included studies reported positive impacts for the majority of reported outcomes in each thematic outcome domain. None of the interventions reported any negative or harmful effects. The strongest degree of evidence was in support for maternal outcomes, and particularly maternal caregiving for nutrition and health. While paternal and couple’s outcomes were relatively less commonly assessed, half of the total evaluated outcome indicated positive impacts of father-inclusive interventions on these outcomes as well. Although child outcomes were the least measured and were associated with the greatest percentage of null results relative to the other categories, results still largely supported overall benefits.

While these results suggest overall family-wide benefits of father-inclusive programs, it is worth noting that only 5 of the 33 programs (15%) comprehensively collected data about a maternal, paternal, couples, and child outcome in their evaluations. The remaining majority of program evaluations collected data about select individuals or sub-systems of the family, which was mostly outcomes about one parent (i.e., mothers) and with more than half not assessing a couples’ or child-level outcome. In particular, programs that enrolled one parent were less likely to measure outcomes about another caregiver besides the individual who was enrolled. More specifically, of the 7 interventions that recruited mothers but still engaged fathers in the program, only 3 (43%) measured paternal outcomes in their evaluation, in comparison to the 58% of overall studies that measured paternal outcomes. Family systems theory underscores the importance of comprehensively and systemically considering outcomes that cover multiple people, roles, and relationships within family contexts. Furthermore, a family systems perspective motivates the importance of approaching, obtaining, and analyzing outcome data collected from multiple family members (Fagan, 2014). Yet half the evaluations included in our review involved only one individual in the family for data collection, which in most cases was the female caregiver. Interviewing multiple individuals – such as both mothers and fathers separately at an individual level but also jointly as ethically appropriate at a family level – and triangulating these diverse perspectives and sources of data in the analysis process can advance our understanding of the family-wide effects of engaging fathers in caregiving interventions. As families in LMICs reflect a diversity of relationships and family structures (e.g., polygamous marriages, multigenerational households) and also include other kinship relationships and caregivers beyond mothers and fathers, future program evaluations in this literature should investigate the effects of male caregiver engagement on the broader family system (e.g., caregiving relationships with and outcomes pertaining to grandparents and siblings) and whether variations in family compositions moderate the effectiveness of fatherhood interventions (Heath et al., 2020; Thuita et al., 2021).

Considering the impacts on caregiver and child-level outcomes together, our review findings point to the possibility that while improving maternal caregiving outcomes are necessary, impacts on maternal outcomes may not fully explain how father-inclusive interventions can translate into improved child outcomes. Indeed, observational studies have shown that young children can achieve greater gains in outcomes when fathers are involved in optimal caregiving in addition to mothers (Jeong et al., 2016). Coparenting and partner relationship dynamics have also been shown to predict both maternal and paternal parenting behaviors as well as mediate relations between parenting and child outcomes (Cabrera et al., 2014). In fact, one of the included intervention studies by J. K. Rempel et al. (2020) in Vietnam conducted a mediation analysis and found that improvements in both paternal and maternal reports of perceived partner support each independently mediated the positive intervention effects of a fatherhood intervention on infant developmental outcome scores. Thus, more concerted efforts to evaluate and improved not only maternal but also paternal caregiving and couple’s relationships dynamics outcomes may facilitate broader changes in overall family relationships that are likely necessary to, in turn, maximize program benefits on child outcomes (Feinberg, 2002).

As part of summarizing the effectiveness of these programs, we extracted details about the measures used in this evidence base to assess maternal, paternal, couples, and child outcomes. Collectively, studies used a broad range of measurement tools and also scored outcome indicators in different ways (e.g., item-level results, subscales, total scale scores). Variability in measurement approaches was particularly apparent for certain types of outcomes, for example paternal caregiving for nutrition and couple’s relationship quality, with no two studies using the same tool or referencing related sources. This could be partly due to the heterogeneity in types of interventions represented and the different ways individual programs aimed to target paternal caregiving for nutrition or couple’s relationship; but could also reflect some uncertainty broadly in the field about what measures are available and which specifically are most optimal for assessing these outcomes. Furthermore, the level of detail provided about these measures also varied considerably across studies, with many studies appearing to use tools that were developed by study authors. Although an assessment of the psychometric properties of these measures was outside the scope of our review, a future literature review of such measures and systematic appraisal of measurement quality (e.g., reliability, validity, if tools were piloted/adapted); their contexts of use (e.g., cross-cultural appropriateness, whether a given measure can be used equivalently with female and male caregivers); and sensitivity for detecting change in the context of fatherhood intervention evaluations will be highly valuable. Ultimately more psychometric evidence and consultations to build consensus with experts and stakeholders (including mothers and fathers themselves from across cultures and context) can help to inform a measurement framework for father-inclusive intervention evaluations in terms of appropriate tools, outcome domains, and tailored for different types of caregiving interventions (e.g., parenting, maternal and child health) (Galle et al., 2021).

While our results highlight a rapidly expanding evidence base suggesting promising program effects of father-inclusive early childhood interventions globally, most interventions were implemented in sub-Saharan Africa, compared to only one study in the Middle East or Latin America. This may partly reflect the fact that sub-Saharan Africa has some of the poorest countries with the lowest gross domestic product (GDP) per capita and to that end receives the largest amount of international donor funding for maternal and child health programs compared to other regions (Arregoces et al., 2019). At the same time, it is also worth recognizing the role of colonialism, neocolonialism, capitalism, patriarchy, and even Western feminist ideals that have propelled a concentration of funding on male engagement for maternal and child wellbeing especially in sub-Saharan Africa (McEwan, 2001). Moreover, most father involvement initiatives in the region have been through vertical programs (e.g., HIV, family planning) that have not addressed or invested in the broader structural determinants (e.g., poverty, unemployment, gender oppression) to fully enable gender equality in a way that is most responsive to the lived experiences of caregivers themselves in LMICs (Cornwall & Rivas, 2015; Dworkin et al., 2015). More fatherhood research and programmatic investments are needed across all regions to design and advance transformative programs that are centered around the lives of both male and female caregivers, leverage broader social and kin relationships (e.g., aunts, uncles, grandparents) that importantly shape family caregiving, and ensure that they are culturally-tailored to the local meanings of fatherhood which vary within and across countries and regions in LMICs (Lansford, 2022; Odimegwu et al., 2020).

There are several limitations worth noting. First, the quality of evidence across studies was relatively weak (small sample sizes, roughly half were not RCTs) contributing to a generally high overall risk of bias. Although none of the studies reported any harmful effects, this could be a result of publication bias in that investigators may be less likely to report null or negative effects and interventions with harmful effects are unlikely to get published. Future intervention evaluations should produce preregistration protocols, which can help to minimize potential threats of publication bias in this evidence base. Second, we may not have captured the full extent of all relevant interventions as we did not also consider qualitative evaluation studies or those published in the grey literature. Third, given our broad focus on father involvement in any type of caregiving intervention for young children, there was a considerable degree of heterogeneity across studies in terms of definitions or lack thereof for fathers and male caregivers; intervention focal areas; level of participation of fathers; types of study outcomes assessed and specific measurement tools (as already mentioned above); and evaluation methods and study designs. This between-study heterogeneity particularly in evaluated outcomes and measurement tools in this relatively small evidence base limited our ability to conduct a meta-analysis and prevented us from exploring whether variations in program implementation characteristics moderated program effectiveness. One included study did test different implementation strategies with fathers as part of its cluster-RCT study design (i.e., group sessions offered to couples versus group sessions combined with home visits for couples) (Luoto et al., 2021). However, these interventions were part of a broader 2×2 factorial design that was not powered to compare differences between these two particular treatment arms involving fathers and authors did not report those results. Considering this rapidly growing literature and an expected increase in the number of program evaluations in the coming years, future reviews will be better positioned to determine whether variation in program dosage, delivery modalities (e.g., mixed gender groups, sex-separated groups), and behavior change strategies (e.g., interactive dialogues, use of media) might explain treatment heterogeneity of father-inclusive interventions and how best to engage fathers across diverse cultural contexts and with respect to the existing systems and services in LMICs.

## Conclusions

This is one of the most comprehensive reviews to explore the effectiveness of interventions that have engaged fathers in caregiving broadly of young children in LMICs and with respect to a broad range of outcomes. From a family systems perspective, our results suggest family-wide benefits of father-inclusive interventions in LMICs for improving outcomes among multiple individuals in the family in the short-term: not only for women and children but also for fathers themselves and couple’s relationships dynamics. At the same time, we underscore the need for more rigorous study designs, longitudinal follow-ups, documentation of the social and cultural factors surrounding fatherhood in the local contexts, and investigation of more explicit fatherhood research questions in program evaluations (e.g., is there an additive effect of targeting fathers compared to mothers?). Greater funding and investments are needed to facilitate new discoveries, replications, adaptations, and eventual scale-up of successful father-involvement interventions across LMICs, especially in under-represented countries and globally across all regions. With more rigorous evaluation designs using standardized outcome measures, we will be better positioned to conduct meta-analyses, derive pooled effect size estimates, and improve our understanding of the effectiveness of father-inclusive interventions.

# Neural correlates of inhibitory control and associations with cognitive outcomes in Bangladeshi children exposed to early adversities

**Authors:** Eileen F Sullivan; Wanze Xie; Stefania Conte; John E Richards; Talat Shama; Rashidul Haque; William A Petri; Charles A Nelson

**Affiliations:** 1 Labs of Cognitive Neuroscience, Division of Developmental Medicine, Boston Children's Hospital, Boston, USA | 2 Harvard Graduate School of Education, Cambridge, USA | 3 School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences, Peking University, Beijing, China | 4 PKU‐IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research, Peking University, Beijing, China | 5 Department of Psychology, University of South Carolina, Columbia, USA | 6 ICDDR, B, Dhaka, Bangladesh | 7 Infectious Diseases & International Health, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, USA | 8 Harvard Medical School, Boston, USA

## Abstract

There is strong support for the view that children growing up in low‐income homes typically evince poorer performance on tests of inhibitory control compared to those growing up in higher income homes. Unfortunately, the vast majority of the work documenting this association has been conducted in high‐income countries. It is not yet known whether the mechanisms found to mediate this association would generalize to children in low‐ and middle‐income countries, where the risks of exposure to extreme poverty and a wide range of both biological and psychosocial hazards may be greater. We examined relations among early adversity, neural correlates of inhibitory control, and cognitive outcomes in 154 5‐year‐old children living in Dhaka, Bangladesh, an area with a high prevalence of poverty. Participants completed a go/no‐go task assessing inhibitory control and their behavioral and event‐related potential responses were assessed. Cortical source analysis was performed. We collected measures of poverty, malnutrition, maternal mental health, psychosocial adversity, and cognitive skills. Supporting studies in high‐income countries, children in this sample exhibited a longer N2 latency and higher P3 amplitude to the no‐go versus go condition. Unexpectedly, children had a more pronounced N2 amplitude during go trials than no‐go trials. The N2 latency was related to their behavioral accuracy on the go/no‐go task. The P3 mean amplitude, behavioral accuracy, and reaction time during the task were all associated with intelligence‐quotient (IQ) scores. Children who experienced higher levels of psychosocial adversity had lower accuracy on the task and lower IQ scores.

Keywords: cognitive development, early adversity, event‐related potentials, inhibitory control, poverty, source analysis

## INTRODUCTION

Executive functions (EF) encompass high‐level cognitive processes that serve as essential building blocks for children's cognitive development, academic achievement, and well‐being (Ahmed et al., 2019; Blair & Razza, 2007; Morgan et al., 2019). Inhibitory control, a core EF skill related to the ability to resist impulsive tendencies and behaviors, is predictive of children's school readiness and social‐emotional skills (Carlson & Wang, 2007; Mann et al., 2017; Rhoades et al., 2009). Associations between socioeconomic status (SES) and inhibitory control have been reliably documented in children, suggesting that inhibitory control is sensitive to environmental inputs (Raver et al., 2013; St. John et al., 2019; Vrantsidis et al., 2020). It is essential to develop a mechanistic understanding of how environmental factors related to SES impact inhibitory control, given the importance of inhibitory control abilities to children's success and well‐being. Discovery of these mechanisms could facilitate the early identification of risk factors and deficits in cognitive functions, informing the design of effective interventions.

Numerous studies have sought to understand what proximal aspects of children's environments may be driving the association between social class and inhibitory control. Several characteristics of the early environment have been found to partially explain the link between SES and inhibition, including parental responsivity, predictability, language exposure, and cognitive stimulation in the home (Hackman et al., 2015; Lecheile et al., 2020; Sarsour et al., 2011). Findings from neuroimaging studies have helped to uncover neural mechanisms of inhibitory control and deepen our understanding of how early experiences shape the development of inhibition (Abdul Brydges et al., 2014; Jonkman, 2006; Rahman et al., 2017). For instance, Swingler et al. (2018) found that maternal emotional support was related to preschoolers’ brain activity during an inhibitory control task, as indexed by the N2 event‐related potential (ERP) component.

The existing evidence base on drivers of SES‐based differences in inhibition is both informative and compelling. However, the vast majority of studies providing this evidence were conducted in high‐income countries (HICs) (Haslam et al., 2019; Lund et al., 2020). It is not yet known whether the mechanisms identified in studies of SES in HICs are generalizable to children growing up in extreme poverty in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs). Children in LMICs are more likely than their HIC‐based peers to be chronically exposed to a broad range of adverse biological factors (e.g., malnutrition, toxin exposure) and psychosocial experiences (e.g., abuse, neglect) that can affect brain structure and function (Benjet, 2010; Donowitz et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2020; Nelson & Gabard‐Durnam, 2020). More evidence from LMICs is needed to explore whether adverse factors associated with extreme poverty uniquely impact the neural and behavioral basis of inhibitory control.

### Research Highlights

- Children living in extreme poverty are exposed to hazards that could compromise inhibitory control skills, yet the underlying neural mechanisms of these impacts are underexplored.

- We measured Bangladeshi children's event‐related potentials and behavioral performance during a go/no‐go task to understand the relations between early adversity and correlates of inhibition.

- Children exhibited lower accuracy and a more pronounced P3 amplitude for trials requiring behavioral inhibition (no‐go condition) than trials requiring no inhibition (go condition).

- The N2 latency was related to higher accuracy on the go/no‐go task. Higher levels of psychosocial adversity were associated with lower accuracy and IQ scores.

Children living in extreme poverty often do not experience just one form of adversity in isolation (Black et al., 2017). A major challenge to investigating associations between adversity on inhibitory control in LMICs is disentangling the unique consequences of co‐occurring risk factors (e.g., malnutrition, abuse, safety risks). Behavioral measures of EF may not be sensitive enough to capture the distinct impacts of multiple adverse factors on inhibitory control. Electrophysiological measures such as electroencephalography (EEG) and ERPs are uniquely positioned to detect how adverse factors are related to the neural mechanisms underlying inhibitory control. There is a need to utilize objective, scalable and (relatively) culture‐free tools in LMICs to investigate relations between early adverse experiences and inhibition. The recordings of EEG activity and the measure of ERPs meet these needs.

Exposure to biological and psychosocial adversity has been reliably linked to consequences on overall brain and cognitive development in LMICs (Jensen et al., 2019; Jensen et al., 2021; Tarullo et al., 2017; Wijeakumar et al., 2019). To develop concrete strategies of prevention and intervention, the mechanisms underlying associations between adversity and development must be understood. Specifically, it is key to identify which aspects of adversity could be impacting the brain structures and functions that subserve the development of inhibitory control. Studies have suggested that disruption to children's expectable psychosocial environments can be linked to the neural and behavioral correlates of inhibition. Psychosocial adversity, encompassing abuse, neglect, family mental illness, and other significant stressors, has been shown to be related to inhibitory control (Cowell et al., 2015; Gueron‐Sela et al., 2018; McDermott et al., 2012). For instance, children experiencing profound early psychosocial deprivation were found to exhibit slower neural responses and diminished accuracy during an ERP go/no‐go task (assessing inhibitory control) as compared to children who had been placed in foster care or had never been institutionalized (McDermott et al., 2012). A follow‐up study of this same sample found that children who remained in neglectful environments performed more poorly than those removed from neglectful situations and placed into family environments on behavioral EF outcomes at 16 years of age, indicating the potentially long‐lasting impacts of extreme neglect (Wade et al., 2019). These findings demonstrate the profound effects of the caregiving environment on the development of inhibition and also highlight the efficacy of employing neuroimaging methods to elucidate mechanisms of the effects of early adversity.

Exposure to maltreatment (e.g., abuse, violence) is another aspect of psychosocial experience that is negatively associated with inhibitory control skills, although further investigation is needed to explore the mechanisms and generalizability of this association (Lund et al., 2020). Associations between child maltreatment and inhibitory control were shown in 3‐ to 9‐year‐old children in the United States; children who experienced maltreatment in infancy or chronically throughout childhood showed poorer performance on inhibitory control tasks (Cowell et al., 2015). In another study of 12‐ to 13‐year‐olds in the US, children who had experienced maltreatment showed atypical ERP responses and lower accuracy during an inhibitory control task as compared to nonmaltreated peers (Bruce & Kim, 2020). Additional studies are needed to investigate whether similar associations between maltreatment and inhibitory control are evident in LMIC populations.

Maternal mental health could also shape children's psychosocial experiences and affect their inhibitory control skills. In one longitudinal study of children in the United States, maternal depression was predictive of preschoolers’ performance on inhibitory control and working memory tasks (Gueron‐Sela et al., 2018). One study in China found that children whose mothers had higher stress levels tended to perform more poorly on inhibitory control tasks at 2 years of age (Liu et al., 2018). These findings, along with others (Hughes et al., 2013; Lund et al., 2020), suggest that maternal mental health is a key feature of the early psychosocial environment that could influence children's inhibitory control abilities. Yet, the neural mechanisms underlying this association are still largely unexplored, especially in LMICs. Importantly, different forms of psychosocial adversity, including neglect, maltreatment, and maternal mental health issues, could co‐occur, but further study of the possible interactive effects of these experiences on inhibition and cognition more broadly is needed.

Along with these potential pathways linking children's psychosocial experiences to inhibitory control, biological risks could also potentially impact children's development of inhibition. Malnutrition is extremely common in many LMICs, and is known to have consequences on children's cognitive development (Ajayi et al., 2017; McCoy et al., 2015). Evidence from interventions suggests a causal link between nutrition and cognitive outcomes, as nutrition supplementation in various forms has been shown to lead to improvements in children's cognitive abilities (Black et al., 2015; Larson & Yousafzai, 2017). Supplementing the behavioral evidence on the pathways linking malnutrition and EF, neuroimaging studies have uncovered possible mechanisms by which malnutrition could impact brain and cognitive development. Micro‐ and macronutrient deficiencies can lead to basic insults on early brain development, leading to persistent effects on brain architecture and functioning (Prado & Dewey, 2014; Turesky et al., 2020). One study in the United States found that nutrition supplementation during the first year of life was associated with differences in ERP responses during an inhibitory control task at 5 years of age (Liao et al., 2017). The consequences of extreme malnutrition on the neural processes underlying inhibitory control have yet to be examined explicitly in LMICs. Furthermore, the impact of co‐occurring biological and psychosocial adversities on inhibition should be explored to reflect the reality that many children experience a complex set of risk factors and protective factors simultaneously.

The current evidence base on the impact of biological and psychosocial exposures serves as an important foundation for understanding children's cognitive development. However, there is a need for further investigation of how early adversity may affect the development of inhibitory control in LMICs. Children living in extreme poverty are at risk of experiencing many forms of adversity simultaneously (Black et al., 2017; Hurley et al., 2016). Therefore, mechanistic evidence on the impact of multiple, potentially interacting adversities is needed to understand which factors have the most profound effects on brain development.

The current study sought to address these gaps in the field by examining how co‐occurring risk factors are related to neural and behavioral correlates of inhibitory control in children living in an impoverished area of Dhaka, Bangladesh. The participants completed study visits at 3 years old and were followed longitudinally at 5 years old. We collected data on SES, maternal mental health, nutrition status, and psychosocial adversity. A cognitive assessment was also conducted. Inhibitory control was assessed when participants were 5 years old using a go/no‐go ERP task, which required children to inhibit behavioral responses to a target stimulus, while EEG data was recorded. The relations among biological and psychosocial risks, ERP components implicated in inhibitory control, behavioral performance on the go/no‐go task, and cognitive abilities were investigated.

Go/no‐go ERP tasks are commonly used in developmental studies (Loman et al., 2013; McDermott et al., 2012, St. John et al., 2019) and offer multiple neural markers to study in relation to early experience and cognitive outcomes. ERPs are electrophysiological signals that are generated in response to a stimulus or task and can index specific aspects of cognitive processing. In this study, we focus on two widely studied ERP components: the N2 and P3. In both children and adults, the N2 peak amplitude and latency (time between stimulus onset and N2 peak amplitude) have been implicated in focused attention, inhibition, and cognitive control; the P3 mean amplitude has been implicated in information processing and inhibitory control (Brydges et al., 2014; Downes et al., 2017; Kopp et al., 2020). Given their role in inhibition and the relations found between early adversity and inhibition, the N2 and P3 could plausibly as objective and sensitive indices of the impact of early adversity on neural circuitry underlying inhibitory control. However, the extent to which the N2 and P3 responses are generalizable across contexts must first be explored. Typically, the N2 has been shown to be generated by the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and prefrontal regions (Bekker et al., 2005; Bokura et al., 2001). The P3 has been localized to precentral and parietal regions (Bokura et al., 2001; Huster et al., 2009). We seek to identify whether the same neural generators of the N2 and P3 are evident in children growing up in an LMIC and infer which brain regions may be driving the association between adversity and inhibitory control skills.

We sought to address three main aims in this study. First, we aimed to assess whether neural markers previously found to underlie inhibitory control are generalizable to our study context by examining the N2 and P3 components. Specifically, we conducted source analysis to probe whether these components are generated from the expected brain regions. Second, to explore potential brain‐behavior relationships in this setting, we investigated whether ERP responses are related to behavioral performance on the go/no‐go task. We also explored whether ERP and behavioral responses during the go/no‐go task are related to overall cognitive functioning, indexed by intelligence quotient (IQ) scores. Finally, to study how early adversity may affect inhibitory control abilities, we investigated whether early adverse factors are predictive of children's ERP responses, behavioral performance on the go/no‐go task, or IQ. We hypothesized that children who experience more extreme adversity would show less typical ERP responses, exhibit poorer inhibitory control, and have lower IQ scores. With the current study, we build off and extend prior evidence on the development of inhibitory control by investigating whether established neural mechanisms of inhibition operate similarly in children growing up in a setting of extreme poverty.

## METHODS

### Participants

Participants live in Dhaka, Bangladesh, and were drawn from two longitudinal cohorts of the Bangladesh Early Adversity Neuroimaging (BEAN) project. One cohort of 130 children (58 females) were originally part of an oral vaccine efficacy trial and were later recruited for the BEAN study at 36 months of age. A second cohort of 80 children (31 females) with a slightly higher average income level were recruited specifically for the BEAN study at 36 months of age. The two cohorts had overlapping distributions of SES and the children were living in the same neighborhood, so all children were treated as one continuous cohort with regard to their SES. All participants had several measures of early adversity collected at 36 and 60 months old and underwent ERP and cognitive tests at 60 months old (M = 62.42, SD = 2.25). Inclusion criteria limited the sample to children born > = 34 weeks gestational age with no history of neurological abnormalities or traumatic brain injury, genetic disorders, or visual or auditory impairments. The final sample for the ERP analyses included 154 children who provided usable ERP data after artifact detection and rejection. Ethical approval was obtained from research and ethics review committees at The International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh and the Institutional Review Board at Boston Children's Hospital. Data were collected in a medical clinic in the Mirpur neighborhood of Dhaka, where local staff were fully trained in behavioral and EEG data collection.

### Stimuli and task procedure

EEG was collected at the 60‐month study visit while children sat approximately 65 cm from a monitor in a dimly lit room and viewed a go/no‐go paradigm. Stimuli and task procedure are shown in Figure 1. Images were presented using E‐Prime 2.0 (Psychological Software products, Harrisburg, PA, USA). The stimuli used in the go/no‐go task consisted of images of four animals common in Bangladesh presented on a white background. Children were told to press a button when they saw a cat, dog, or cow (go trials), but not when they saw a chicken (no‐go trials). Children first completed 15 practice trials with feedback and 15–30 trials with no feedback. Next, the task consisted of 170 trials with no feedback, of which 70% were go trials and 30% were no‐go trials. Each trial consisted of the image of an animal presented for 1000 ms, followed by a blank white screen presented for 1000–1300 ms (randomized). Participants’ looking behavior was monitored and recorded using a Tobii X2‐60 eye‐tracking system. Behavioral responses (button presses) during the paradigm were recorded. Average accuracy was calculated for all trials and each condition separately. Mean reaction time was computed for correct go trials and incorrect no‐go trials, as these are the trials for which the child pressed the button.

### EEG data collection, processing, and analysis

Continuous EEG was recorded while participants viewed the paradigm using a 128‐channel HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net (HGSN) with a NetAmps 300 high‐input amplifier (Electrical Geodesic Inc., Eugene, OR). Impedances were limited to a maximum of 100 kΩ and data was sampled at 500 Hz from all electrodes. EEG data was filtered with a 0.3–30 Hz finite impulse response (FIR) bandpass filter in ERPLAB (Lopez‐Calderon & Luck, 2014). The recordings were segmented into epochs from 100 ms before stimulus onset to 900 ms following stimulus onset. Segmented data was visually inspected and epochs containing artifacts due to eye‐movements, eye‐blinks, or drift were rejected. Segmented data was also automatically removed in ERPLAB using absolute or stepwise criteria (EEG amplitude < −100 or > 100 μV or change in EEG > 100 μV in a 100 ms moving window with 50 ms steps). Individual electrodes with a voltage change exceeding 200 μV were rejected. Epochs were automatically rejected if 18 or more electrodes were removed due to voltage change. For trials with fewer than 18 electrodes removed, individual electrodes were linearly interpolated with the five closest usable electrodes weighted by their distances to the bad electrode (Xie & Richards, 2016; Xie & Richards, 2017). Data were referenced to an average reference after artifact rejection and channel interpolation. Only go and no‐go trials with correct behavioral responses were used in analyses of the stimulus‐locked ERP components. The average number of acceptable trials was 89.29 (SD = 13.68) for the go condition and 31.81 (SD = 7.59) for the no‐go condition. An equal number of acceptable trials for each condition were randomly selected (e.g., including a random subset of acceptable go trials to match the number of acceptable no‐go trials). Participants’ data was removed from further analysis if there were fewer than 10 acceptable trials for each condition. Out of the 210 participants originally enrolled, 154 participants contributed acceptable ERP data and were therefore included in final analyses. Of the 56 participants who were not included, 34 did not participate in EEG, 14 had technical issues during data collection, and eight did not have enough included trials per condition.

Data from multiple electrodes were averaged into seven clusters to assess ERPs from regions commonly associated with EF (Table S1). The mean P3 amplitude was defined as the average response from 400 to 700 ms for each condition and was calculated for the Parietal_Left, Parietal_Z, Parietal_Right, and Central_Z clusters. Peak N2 amplitude, defined as the peak response from 250 to 500 ms for each condition, and latency to peak N2 amplitude were calculated for the Frontal_Left, Frontal_Z, Frontal_Right, and the Central_Z clusters. We used the mean amplitude for the P3 component because many children at this age do not have a clear P3 peak. In contrast, the peak of the N2 component at this age is sharp and easy to identify. Thus, peak amplitudes provide a comparison between experimental conditions at their maxima. A similar approach has been implemented in previous ERP studies investigating perceptual and cognitive processes in young children, that is, using the peak amplitude and latency for the N290 component but mean amplitude for the P400 and Nc components (Xie et al., 2019). The normalized difference between conditions, calculated for each ERP component as the difference between the no‐go and go condition divided by the mean of the two conditions, was used when testing associations between ERP components and adversity measures or behavioral outcomes.

### Cortical source analysis

Cortical source analysis was computed using Fieldtrip (Oostenveld et al., 2011) functions to solve the forward and inverse problems. Custom MATLAB scripts (adapted from https://osf.io/knf9t/, Conte & Richards, 2021a) were implemented to obtain the distribute current source density and perform data reduction to a set of selected regions of interest (ROIs) implicated in inhibitory control tasks (Bekker et al., 2005; Bokura et al., 2001). Figure 2 displays the set of ROIs selected for the current study. Realistic head models were created using individual MRIs when available (n = 78), whereas MRIs close in size to the participants’ head were utilized when own imaging data was unavailable (n = 76). MRIs were acquired at the National Institute for Neuroscience and Hospital (NINSH) in Dhaka, Bangladesh using a 3 T Siemens MAGNETOM Verio scanner. Structural T1‐weighted magnetization‐prepared rapid gradient‐echo (MPRAGE) scans were acquired with the following parameters: TR = 2500 ms, TE = 3.47 ms, 176 sagittal slices, 1 mm3 voxels, FOV = 256 mm.

*FIGURE 2: Atlas of 16 regions of interest displayed on the age‐appropriate MRI template*

All MRIs were segmented into nine tissue types (i.e., gray matter, white matter, cerebrospinal fluid, dura, skull, muscle, eyes, nasal cavity, and scalp) to provide an accurate description of the head's compartments (Conte et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2019; Guy et al., 2016; Xie & Richards, 2017). We generated tetrahedrons wireframe grids and a finite element method (FEM) head model with source dipoles restricted to the gray matter and eyes (Conte & Richards, 2021b). Electrode placements were defined based on the coordinates of five fiducial markers placed on the scalp using the pictures of each participant's net placement. Then, the coordinates of all electrodes were reconstructed and coregistered with the MRI. The inverse solution was estimated using the exact‐LORETA method (eLORETA; Pascual‐Marqui, 2007; Pascual‐Marqui et al., 2011) and applied to the ERP dataset. A singular value decomposition (SVD) was performed at each location of the source model to obtain a measure of the reconstructed source at each timepoint of the ERP segment. SVD values of both experimental conditions were then averaged within each ROI. For visualization purposes, the individual source solutions were normalized to an age‐appropriate MRI template. The source activity at the peak of each component was averaged across participants and displayed on the MRI template space.

### Measures of early adversity

#### Poverty

Household poverty was assessed from items on a sociodemographic questionnaire administered at 36 months of age. A cumulative sum score was constructed to measure household poverty. This score included (1) income‐to‐needs ratio; (2) housing risks and assets as observed during a home visit including flooring materials, wall materials, roof materials, presence of cooking gas, toilet type, private versus shared toilet, open drain in from of house, municipality provided water supply, and crowding (> 3 people per room); and (3) a count of common family assets noted by an observer during a home visit including presence of a bed, table, chair, bench, phone, clock, radio, television, bicycle, motorcycle, sewing machine, and fan. The average daily income was $2.18 (SD = 2.11) per household member, with 64% of families living in extreme poverty, defined by the World Bank as living on less than $1.90 per person per day. See Table S2 for full descriptive statistics.

#### Malnutrition

To assess malnutrition, children's height was measured at 36 months of age and used to calculate their height‐for‐age z‐score (HAZ) using the World Health Organization's Anthro Plus software (version 3.2.2). A subset of participants (n = 104) had HAZ measured at 60 months of age as well; HAZ was highly correlated between the 36‐month and 60‐month timepoint (r(104) = 0.90, p < 0.001). Children had an average HAZ of −1.33 (SD = 1.04) at 36 months of age, and 26% of children met the criteria for stunting (HAZ < −2).

#### Maternal mental health

Mothers’ level of psychological stress and depression was measured when participants were 36 months old using a cumulative summary score of three questionnaires: the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) (Gausia et al., 2007), the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) (Cohen et al., 1983), and the Tension Scale (Karasz et al., 2013). The Bengali version of the EPDS was validated in a Bangladeshi sample (Gausia et al., 2007) and was used in this study after the local psychologists added select colloquial terminologies as options for administration. The PSS was translated to Bengali by two bilingual psychologists separately. The translations were reviewed by a team of experts and nonstudy mothers; a first version of the translated PSS was field tested, modified to clarify points of confusion reported by mothers, and back translated and matched to the original version. Pretesting of the Bengali version of the PSS was conducted with 14 mothers and showed a test‐retest reliability score after a 7‐day gap was r = 0.86. The Tension Scale was developed specifically for Bangladeshi women (Karasz et al., 2013) and was used in the current study with no further modifications. The three questionnaires were highly interrelated in this sample (Cronbach's α = 0.721), and therefore scores on the three scales were summed to create a summary score encapsulating overall mental health and well‐being. The average maternal stress summary score was 52.26 (SD = 17.23).

#### Psychosocial adversity

Children's cumulative exposure to adverse psychosocial experiences was assessed using the Childhood Psychosocial Adversity Scale (CPAS), a parent‐reported questionnaire developed specifically for the study population, when children were 60 months old (Berens et al., 2019). The CPAS was informed by qualitative work with Bangladeshi mothers and field workers, designed in collaboration with local psychologists, and pretested in the current study setting. The questionnaire includes nine subscales: harsh discipline and abuse, neglect, caregiver emotional availability, depression, social isolation, physical intimate partner violence, verbal abuse and family conflict, household economic stress, and community adversity. The CPAS has been shown to have good internal consistency for all subscales in the BEAN sample (Cronbach's alpha > 0.7). For the purpose of these analyses, the full‐scale score (simple sum of all subscales) was used as an index of cumulative exposure. The average score on the CPAS was 39.33 (SD = 21.66).

### Cognitive assessment

Children's cognitive development was assessed by local psychologists when children were 60 months of age using the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Third Edition (WPPSI‐III) (Wechsler, 1991). The WPPSI was adapted to the Bangladeshi context and has been shown to be locally acceptable (Aboud, 2007). For the current analyses, full‐scale IQ was used as a measure of overall higher‐order cognitive functioning. Full‐scale IQ was strongly correlated with both performance IQ (r(152) = 0.88, p < 0.001) and verbal IQ subscales (r(152) = 0.85, p < 0.001). Children's mean full‐scale IQ score on the WPPSI was 86.94 (SD = 9.33).

### Statistical approach

To address study aim one, ERP components of interest (N2 peak amplitude and latency, P3 mean amplitude) were analyzed using a repeated‐measures analyses of variance (RM‐ANOVAs) were performed with condition and electrode cluster as within‐subject factors. Greenhouse‐Geisser corrections were applied when necessary to control for violations of sphericity. Post‐hoc t‐testing was performed to investigate which electrode clusters revealed significant condition differences. Bonferroni corrections for multiple comparisons were performed. T tests were used to assess condition‐differences (go vs. no‐go) in reaction time and accuracy.

To address study aim two, Pearson correlations were used to investigate possible associations among ERP components, reaction time, accuracy, and IQ. Multiple linear regressions were used to assess study aim three concerning whether measures of early adversity were related to ERP components of interest, behavioral performance on the go/no‐go task, or IQ. RM‐ANOVAs were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 27, IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA). Correlations and regressions were performed using RStudio (version 1.3.1093, Boston, MA, USA).

### Behavioral performance

In line with prior studies, children had higher mean accuracy for go trials (86.40%) than no‐go trials (72.57%), t(277.48) = 9.49, p < 0.001. Children's average reaction time was faster for incorrect trials (0.71 s) than correct trials (0.75 s), t(220.51) = 2.34, p = 0.02 (see Figure 3).

### ERP responses

#### N2 findings

The RM‐ANOVA of the N2 peak amplitude revealed significant main effects of electrode cluster, F(2.48, 379.05) = 48.81, p < 0.001, and go versus no‐go condition, F(1, 153) = 453.17, p < 0.001 . A significant interaction effect between electrode cluster and condition was also found, F(2.51, 384.25) = 110.86, p < 0.001 (see Figure 4). After correcting for multiple comparisons, the N2 peak amplitude in Frontal_Z (midline), Frontal_Right, and Central_Z electrode clusters was significantly greater (more negative) for the go condition than the no‐go condition (p‐values < 0.001). In contrast, the N2 peak amplitude in the Frontal_Left cluster was significantly more negative for the no‐go condition compared to the go condition (p < 0.001). Because all clusters showed significant condition differences, the difference between the go and no‐go N2 peak amplitude in these four clusters were averaged together and used in further analyses.
